title: Reading Primary Sources Critically: the Boston Massacre
subtitle: Sourcing, corroboration and cautious claims, practised on accounts of King Street, 5 March 1770

learner.topic: Historical source analysis: reading primary sources critically, using the Boston Massacre (5 March 1770) as the case
goals: Identify a source's author, audience, date and purpose and explain how they shape what it says
Compare two accounts of the same event and explain their disagreements with evidence
Write a short evidence-based claim that acknowledges competing interpretations
learner.scope: Method of source criticism applied to one event; not a full history of the American Revolution
exclusions: Full narrative history of the Revolution

learner.startingKnowledge: Adult self-learner; enjoys history podcasts; no training in historical method

sources.evidenceStandard: Primary sources from authoritative archives/editions (Library of Congress, Massachusetts Historical Society, Founders Online / National Archives) plus recognized scholarship for context

assumptions: Synthetic learner profile used only to demonstrate the format
Unknown: learner.background beyond podcasts; examples assume no knowledge of the Revolution beyond a general outline (a short context box is provided)

modules.title: Sourcing: who made this and why?
modules.summary: Ask four questions of any source before trusting or dismissing it.

modules.title: Corroboration and cautious claims

glossary.definition: Material created at the time being studied (or by someone who lived it): a letter, newspaper report, print, deposition. Primary is a role relative to your question, not a type of object.
Work that interprets primary sources after the fact, such as a historian's book or an encyclopedia entry.
Asking who made a source, for whom, when and why, before deciding what to make of its content.
The documented origin and history of a source: who made it, how it was published or kept, and how it reached us.
The people a source was meant to reach. Audience changes what an author includes, stresses or leaves out.
What the author hoped the source would do: persuade, defend, record, mourn, sell. A purpose does not make a source false; it tells you what to check.
A conclusion you draw from evidence rather than something a source states outright. Good history labels inferences as such.
Checking a claim against other independent sources. Agreement among sources that copied each other is not independent confirmation.
A sworn statement taken from a witness, often collected by one side of a dispute to support its case.
Disputed among sources or among historians, as opposed to established (well supported across sources) or unknown.
An explanation of what happened or why, built from evidence. Several interpretations can be defensible when the evidence is thin or conflicting.
A statement you assert and support with cited evidence. A well-made claim states how confident it is.
A print made by cutting an image into a metal plate, inking it and pressing paper onto it, so many copies can be sold. Prints could spread an image quickly and cheaply.

routes.title: Core route
routes.description: Both available lessons in order, then the capstone. Two 45-minute sessions plus the capstone.

intro:
Podcasts and documentaries hand you conclusions. Historians work from sources: things people wrote, printed or drew at the time, each made by someone, for someone, for a reason. This course teaches a small, reusable method for reading such sources and for saying what they do and do not show. The case is the shooting in King Street, Boston, on 5 March 1770, because it left us unusually rival accounts, made within weeks of each other by people who wanted different outcomes.

How it works. Each lesson is built for one 45-minute session: you try before you are told, compare your answer with a model, and write short answers in your own words. Open-ended questions have rubrics and model answers, not answer keys, because on this topic several conclusions can be defensible. The course is a guided start (about 1.5 hours of material in this version, with more lessons planned); the full plan is about 3 hours.

Prerequisites. None beyond curiosity. Background in one box: in 1770 Boston was garrisoned by British soldiers, and many residents resented their presence. Tension had risen over the preceding days.

diagnostic.intro: Three quick questions on how you already read sources. They only suggest a pace; nothing is hidden from you.

questions.prompt: A letter written by a participant the day after an event is…
options: Always reliable because it is so close in time
A primary source whose author, audience and purpose still need checking
A secondary source because it is only one person's view
questions.explanation: Closeness in time helps but does not remove motive or limited vantage point. A participant's letter is a primary source.

feedback.0: Closeness in time is a plus, not a guarantee: the writer may have been frightened, mistaken, or trying to shape what others believe.
feedback.2: Primary/secondary is about when and by whom it was made, not about how many viewpoints it holds.

questions.prompt: Two reports of the same event disagree about who started it. The best first move is…
options: Pick the one that seems more neutral
Ask who made each, for whom and why, and what else could settle the point
questions.explanation: Disagreement is a starting point for explaining differences with evidence, not a signal to pick a winner by tone.

feedback.0: Neutral tone is easy to fake and is not evidence.
feedback.1: Facts do not average; one claim may be wrong or both may be partial.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most carefully worded claim?
options: The sources prove the crowd was a mob.
Given that the accounts conflict and both have reasons to persuade, the evidence here does not settle who gave the order.
questions.explanation: It names the evidence situation and states its limit instead of overreaching.

capstone.title: Capstone: a short argument with competing interpretations
capstone.task:
Question: Were the events of 5 March 1770 better understood as a deliberate massacre of civilians by soldiers, or as a chaotic confrontation in which soldiers panicked?

Write 250 to 350 words. You must: (1) state your claim and how confident you are; (2) use at least two sources from the course (for example Preston's account, the 12 March Boston-Gazette report, the Revere engraving), citing each by author, date and archive link; (3) for each source, say in one sentence how its author, audience and purpose affect what it says; (4) present at least one competing interpretation fairly and explain why you still prefer yours or why you suspend judgment; (5) name one piece of evidence that would change your mind.

You may choose a different supported claim if you justify it, but you may not claim certainty about the order to fire.

descriptors: Treats sources as simply true or simply biased
Names author or date but does not connect them to what the source says
For each source, connects author, audience, date and purpose to specific features of its content
Cites sources but loosely or without distinguishing quotation from inference
Cites precisely, separates what a source says from what you infer, and notes gaps
Mentions another view without engaging it
States a rival interpretation fairly and explains why the evidence does or does not favor yours
Overstates (proves, obviously) or refuses to conclude anything
Some hedging, not tied to the evidence
Confidence matches the strength of evidence and says what would change it

capstone.evaluation: Human judgment is needed. The browser cannot grade an essay. Self-assess with the rubric first. Then ask a person (a friend who reads history, a tutor, or a study group) to read your text and the rubric and say, for each criterion, which level they see and quote the sentence that shows it. If they cannot find a competing interpretation presented fairly, revise. Do not rely on a language model to grade this either; its confident feedback is not evidence about your reasoning.
capstone.model:
One defensible exemplar (not the only one). “My claim, held with moderate confidence, is that the evidence best supports a confused confrontation rather than a planned massacre, but the sources cannot settle who gave the order to fire. Captain Preston, writing to persuade a British audience while under charge, says his words were "Don't fire, stop your Firing"; the 12 March Boston-Gazette report says "the Captain commanded them to fire". Each account fits its author’s position, so neither can be taken at face value, and neither is independent of the other’s aims. A rival reading, that the soldiers acted on an order and the event was a deliberate act of force, takes the Gazette at its word; it is defensible, but it rests on one printed report whose author and sources are not stated on the archive page. What would change my mind: a signed, independent sworn statement from a close witness agreeing with one account.”

Note what the exemplar does: it quotes briefly, ties each account to purpose, states a rival, and says what evidence would shift it. A claim favoring the Gazette reading, supported as carefully, would also reach Proficient.
